title: Beta-blockers and alpha-blockers compared: heart, airway and pressure
ariaLabel: Schematic comparing adrenergic blockers: beta-1 receptors in the heart, beta-2 receptors in the airway, and alpha-1 receptors in vessels. Propranolol blocks both beta receptors, metoprolol mostly beta-1, carvedilol and labetalol block beta and alpha-1, nebivolol blocks beta-1 and adds nitric oxide release, pindolol is a partial agonist, and prazosin blocks only alpha-1.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.

nodes.label: Sympathetic signal
nodes.info: Noradrenaline and adrenaline reaching beta-1 receptors on heart cells. The slider sets the level.

nodes.label: Vessel alpha-1 signal
nodes.info: Noradrenaline acting on alpha-1 receptors of vessel muscle.

nodes.label: Endothelial nitric oxide
nodes.info: Nitric oxide made by the vessel lining, which widens vessels.

nodes.label: Sympathetic signal
nodes.info: Noradrenaline and adrenaline reaching beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle.

nodes.label: Airway relaxed
nodes.info: Beta-2 signalling relaxes airway smooth muscle.

nodes.label: Heart rate and force
nodes.info: A teaching score for heart rate and force of contraction, driven by beta-1 receptors in the heart.

nodes.label: Blood pressure
nodes.info: A teaching score for blood pressure, from cardiac output and vessel tone.

nodes.label: Airway width
nodes.info: A teaching score for how wide the airway is, kept open by beta-2 receptors on airway muscle.

edges.label: beta-1 receptor
edges.info: Beta-1 blockade lowers heart rate and force. Selective blockers (metoprolol type) act mostly here; non-selective blockers and carvedilol or labetalol also block beta-2.
More heart stimulation raises heart rate and force.

edges.label: alpha-1 receptor
edges.info: Alpha-1 blockade (carvedilol, labetalol, prazosin) widens vessels, which lowers pressure and can cause a fall on standing.

edges.label: NO release
edges.info: Nebivolol raises nitric oxide release from the vessel lining in addition to beta-1 blockade, which widens vessels. Most other beta-blockers do not.

edges.label: beta-2 receptor
edges.info: Beta-2 blockade lets the airway muscle tighten. This is why non-selective blockers are avoided in asthma; selective blockers are safer, though not risk-free.

edges.label: cardiac output
edges.info: A faster, stronger heart raises pressure.

sources: Where each class acts. Propranolol type blocks beta-1 and beta-2, metoprolol type mostly beta-1, carvedilol and labetalol add alpha-1 blockade, nebivolol adds nitric oxide release, pindolol is a partial agonist, and prazosin blocks only alpha-1. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Intrinsic sympathomimetic activity in detail, membrane stabilising effect, lipid solubility and brain effects, half-lives, the benefit in heart failure and after infarction, cautions (asthma, heart block, diabetes, abrupt stopping), alpha-2 effects and the reflex rise in sympathetic drive are left out. Heart rate, airway width and pressure are teaching scores. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
